opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think I had some grand prophetic moment where I looked at it and said, "This is going to change the world." It was much more gradual than that.

When I joined OpenAI, I was mostly thinking about reinforcement learning and infrastructure. That's my background: I'd built Tianshou, and I cared a lot about making RL systems run fast and correctly. Inside the company there was this effort to take the language models we already had and make them actually follow instructions and talk to people, using human feedback and RL. To me that was interesting first as an engineering problem. You have a huge model, you have a reward model, you have this messy RL loop, and you need the whole thing to be stable and efficient. That's exactly the kind of thing I like working on.

What really convinced me was using it myself. When you play with the base model, it's impressive but kind of wild. It continues text, it doesn't really listen to you. After the RLHF post-training, you could just ask it things, and it would try to help. Not perfectly, it made lots of mistakes, but the jump in usability was very obvious. I remember thinking: if I, as someone who sees all the flaws, still want to use this every day, then normal people will probably find it even more useful.

There was also a simple bet in my head: the infrastructure for post-training was going to matter a lot, and not many people wanted to do the unglamorous parts, like making the training loop reliable, debugging weird reward hacking, and making iteration fast. If I could make the researchers iterate ten times faster, that would compound. So I thought, okay, even if the product itself doesn't take off, the capability we're building is real, and the work will be valuable.

Then it launched and blew up far beyond what any of us expected. So I'd say I recognized it was worth the effort, but I definitely did not predict how big it would become. Nobody on the team really did.

r001.rationale: The response cites personal daily use and ChatGPT’s unexpectedly large launch as signals, but does not identify users spontaneously promoting it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I recognized it in the way that word implies, like some clear-eyed moment where I saw the future. It was much messier than that.

I joined OpenAI in 2022, and at that point the project that became ChatGPT wasn't a big strategic bet inside the company. It was a fairly small group of people, and the framing was more like, let's take the models we already have and make them conversational, make them easier for ordinary people to talk to. The research side was already pretty mature. GPT-3 existed, instruction tuning existed, RLHF existed. What was missing was that a normal person couldn't actually sit down and use any of it without reading documentation and poking at an API.

I came from a reinforcement learning background. I'd built Tianshou, which is an RL library, so I was comfortable with the training loop side of things. But what pulled me in was something simpler. I remember the first time I used an early internal version and just started asking it questions the way I'd ask a colleague, and it answered in a way that felt like it understood what I meant rather than just completing text. That gap between "this is a text completion engine" and "this feels like a conversation" seemed small on paper, but it felt enormous when you actually experienced it.

So I think the honest answer is that I didn't invest because I predicted a hundred million users. I invested because the problem was concrete and I could see exactly where I could help. There was a lot of unglamorous infrastructure work, making the model serve fast enough, making the training pipeline reliable, dealing with the fact that nobody had really productionized this kind of thing before. Those are problems I like. And I had this slight feeling that if we got it right, people who had never thought about AI would suddenly be using it every day. I wouldn't call it a prediction. It was more like a hunch that the hard research part was done and the thing standing between the model and the world was engineering, and engineering is something you can actually just go do.

In hindsight people like to tell a clean story, but internally there was real uncertainty right up until launch about whether anyone outside the company would care. I think a lot of us were genuinely surprised at how fast it took off. So if I recognized anything, it was that the gap between what the technology could do and what people could access was unusually large, and closing that gap was worth my time regardless of how it played out.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a hunch that ordinary people might use ChatGPT every day and surprise at its rapid takeoff, but does not identify users spontaneously promoting it as a reason to invest effort.

astra-6.text: For me, it was the gap between hearing about it and actually trying it. I could ask a question, follow up, and refine an idea in the same conversation. That felt like a different way of working with a computer. It wasn’t perfect, but I could see how useful it could become. I didn’t know exactly where it would lead, but I felt that spending time learning how to use it was worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites its own experience asking follow-up questions and refining ideas as the reason to invest effort. It does not identify users spontaneously promoting ChatGPT as a signal.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was the experience of using it. You could ask a question in ordinary language, follow up, and get help with something you were actually working on. That made it feel different from a tool you try once and forget about. I started seeing more and more things I wanted to use it for, and that was the signal: if it was already useful, it was worth spending time learning what else it could do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says its own growing use of ChatGPT signaled it was worth learning, but does not identify users spontaneously promoting it.
